newsitem.title: TAIWAN: No change seen in China's post-Deng Taiwan policy.
newsitem.headline: No change seen in China's post-Deng Taiwan policy.

text.p: Seen from Taiwan, the heirs of Deng Xiaoping show no sign of diverging from the late paramount leader's carrot-and-stick strategy for bringing the wayward island under communist China's red flag.
Beijing appears undeterred in its readiness to use its modernising army to end what Deng and Mao Zedong before him saw as Nationalist-ruled Taiwan's unnatural estrangement from the motherland.
A 14.7 percent 1997 defence budget increase unveiled in China's parliament on Sunday was widely interpreted as posing little new threat to anyone in Asia -- except for Taiwan.

Under Deng, who died on February 19 at age 92, China offered several carrots to win back Taiwan, the last stronghold of the exiled Republic of China government since its defeat by Mao's communists on the mainland in 1949.

The most alluring is an open door for Taiwan in China's booming economy, a policy that has attracted more than US$20 billion in investment from 30,000 Taiwan enterprises and significantly enriched the island in the process.

A second carrot is time -- Beijing's willingness to leave the political stalemate alone until conditions for reunification improve on the condition that Taipei does nothing that China might construe as a move toward independence.

The ultimate carrot in Deng's eyes and his successors' is an offer of unification under a "one country, two systems" model promising Taiwan and Hong Kong a high degree of autonomy on condition they accept the communist government's sovereignty.
Britain accepted the model for Hong Kong's July 1 return to Chinese rule. Taiwan has rejected it outright, saying political liberalisation on the mainland must precede reunification.

At the first of a likely flurry of "China after Deng" forums in Taipei on Monday, China-watchers said Deng largely achieved his aim of forging a stabilising "collective leadership" to take over the near-imperial clout wielded by Deng and Mao.

"In the post-Deng period, there may be minor instability or disturbances on the mainland, but I think major turmoil is unlikely," said Chiu Chuang-huan, a senior adviser to Taiwan President Lee Teng-hui.
In the absence of major political upheaval, experts said, China's policy toward Taiwan was likely to change little -- as long as Taiwan itself does not provoke its giant rival.

"Taiwan itself can introduce new problems to the situation in the Taiwan Strait (separating the island from the mainland) but it can't alter the situation in China proper," said highly regarded Beijing-watcher Yang Kai-huang.

Yang said China would exploit this dynamic, swiftly checking more provocative moves such as Taiwan's seeking a U.N. seat or making top-level visits to Japan or the United States, while at the same time not acting too aggressively towards Taipei.

Beijing's eight months of live-fire war games and missile tests near Taiwan after President Lee managed to make an unofficial U.S. visit in June 1995 made clear just how little room it was willing to give the island.

Defence analysts say China's US$9.7 billion defence budget aims to boost logistics in the three million-strong People's Liberation Army (PLA), still seen as lacking the sophistication needed for a quick, decisive and politically defensible attack on the heavily armed island.
"They say they want the ability to fight a high-tech war under modern conditions," said Taiwan PLA-watcher Arthur Ding.
"Although this would be useful against Japan or other Asian neighbours, there is no doubt that Taiwan is the first target."

Taiwan has stepped up buying advanced arms to counter the PLA's modernisation, laying in U.S. F-16 and French Mirage fighters and U.S. Patriot anti-missile missiles, though Beijing's angry responses prompted Paris to agree to stop arming Taiwan.

When China's war games escalated on the eve of Taiwan's historic March 1996 presidential election, Washington stepped in to preserve the military balance by dispatching two aircraft carriers to the region in a dramatic warning to Beijing.
Experts nevertheless cautioned that today's stable balance could tilt to Beijing's advantage if an apparent easing of longstanding U.S.-China frictions gains significant momentum.
"If U.S. interests tip strongly in favour of the mainland and away from Taiwan, there is some risk for Taiwan," said China-watcher Yang.
